name: Drubea
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Lionnet, Florian. 2025. Tonal languages without tone: downstep in Drubea and Numèè (Oceanic, New Caledonia). Phonology 42: e23, 1-43. doi:10.1017/S0952675725100171 (Cambridge Core, CC-BY 4.0 open access)
catalog_locator: §6.2 'Tone, register and the typology of word-prosodic systems', pp. 39-40; lexical register classes of disyllables: §3.6 p. 19 ex. (34); abstract p. 1; identity §2.1 p. 3
catalog_quote: Given that register is not tone stricto sensu, and given that the register feature l in Drubea and Numèè is culminative (no more than one per stem), which is a property frequently associated with ‘accent’, one may hypothesize that Drubea and Numèè might be better described as accentual rather than tonal languages. I show in this section that this is not the case ... Neither of Hyman’s (2006) inviolable criteria is met: downstep is not obligatory in Drubea and Numèè, where many stems (and words) contain only registerless RBUs, that is, have no indication of register. Downstep is also not syllable-dependent: the RBU is the mora (although the syllable plays an important role in determining which mora in a CVV syllable is the RBU). Finally, downstep in Drubea and Numèè is not demarcative, since it is found on both the first and second syllables of disyllabic stems; that is, its position within a stem does not seem to be defined or constrained by a reference to either edge of the stem. ... Given this definition, Drubea and Numèè can be classified as bona fide tonal languages: their word-prosodic system is entirely based on a lexical pitch-based contrast which has a morpheme as its domain – specifically the stem

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (text extraction, lines 2163-2218 = article sec. 6.2 'Tone, register and the typology of word-prosodic systems', pp. 39-40). The quoted passage is there word for word; the two '[..]' elisions cover (a) the parenthesis '(although the syllable plays an important role in determining which mora in a CVV syllable is the RBU)' and (b) the intervening sentences defining TONE per Hyman 2006: 229; the final clause continues ': their word-prosodic system is entirely based on a lexical pitch-based contrast which has a morpheme as its domain'. Surrounding section read: Lionnet raises the hypothesis that the culminative downstep might make Drubea/Numee 'accentual rather than tonal', tests it agains…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Drubea is a tone (register) language: the word-prosodic system consists solely of a lexically specified downstep (traditionally 'low/marked tone' vs 'high') on a mora of the stem; at most one downstep per stem, but many stems have none, and in disyllables it may sit on either the first or the second syllable (three lexical classes /σσ/, /ꜜσσ/, /σꜜσ/), so its position is unpredictable and not edge-bound. The author explicitly argues this is not a stress-accent system. No opened source states where (non-contrastive) word stress falls; Gordon & Maddieson 1999 and the ALK likewise only say the language is tonal (two tones, low marked).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Recent loanwords from French/English form a fourth class with downstep always inside the initial long syllable (CVꜜV.CV(V), e.g. /oꜜoci/ 'horse', /kaꜜaʈɛ/ 'car'; §3.7 p. 27). Verbal classifier prefixes copy the register of the verb-initial syllable; compounds may contain more than one downstep. Utterance-final raising (Drubea) vs utterance-final downstepping (Numèè) are postlexical.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain of the lexical contrast is the stem/morpheme (register-bearing unit = mora); realisation described within utterances (pitch relative to the preceding syllable), with postlexical pre-downstep raising (upstep) and utterance-final effects. Analysis rests on Rivierre 1973 transcriptions (Unya dialect) plus the author's pitch tracings of Shintani's 1990s Païta-area recordings; the author collected no new data.
new_statements.identity_note: Lionnet 2025 describes Drubea (dumb1241) and Numèè (nucl1484) jointly as one word-prosodic system ('virtually identical', differing only in utterance-final phenomena); his Drubea data come second-hand from Rivierre 1973 (Unya dialect, north of Yaté) and from Shintani & Païta 1990 / Shintani 2019 recordings (Païta-area speakers). Gordon & Maddieson 1999 recorded speakers at Naniouni (west coast) and Unya. Language names in the sources: Drubea, nraa/nââ drubea, Ndumbea, Païta, langue d'Unya — all dumb1241.

tone_statements.citation: Shintani, Tadahiko L. A. 2009. Le nráa drùbea comme langue à tons. Causerie (public lecture) for Les amis du Musée de Nouvelle-Calédonie, Musée de Nouvelle-Calédonie, Nouméa, 23 September 2009; author's abstract published online by the Service du Musée de la Nouvelle-Calédonie. (Cited in Entrelangues as: Shintani, T. 2009. 'Le nraa drubea: langue à plusieurs tons', présentation à l'université de Nouvelle-Calédonie.)
tone_statements.quote: J’ai travaillé longtemps sur l’une des langues de l’extrême-sud,nráa drùbea, mais la difficulté de décrier le système tonal de cette langue demeure toujours. J’ai l’impression qu’il faut tenir compte de deux facteurs prosodiques: ton syllabique isolé et la mélodie qui couvre plusieur syllables. Il est certain que cette langue a deux tons ponctuel (haut et bas), mais le ton syllabique isolé est souvent modifié par la mélodie intersyllabique. Ce système tonal a un aspect semblabe au système “accentuel” du japonais qui n’a toutefois pas de tons syllabiques isolés.
tone_statements.translation: I have worked for a long time on one of the far-south languages, nráa drùbea, but the difficulty of describing this language's tonal system remains. My impression is that two prosodic factors must be taken into account: the isolated syllabic tone and the melody that covers several syllables. It is certain that this language has two punctual (level) tones (high and low), but the isolated syllabic tone is often modified by the intersyllabic melody. This tonal system has an aspect similar to the 'accentual' system of Japanese, which however has no isolated syllabic tones.
tone_statements.locator: online abstract, section 'Le nráa drùbea comme langue à tons', 3rd paragraph (museum causerie page dated 23 septembre 2009)
tone_statements.summary: 2 level tones (H, L) on syllables, overlaid/modified by a multi-syllable word melody; author likens it to Japanese pitch accent; analysis explicitly unresolved (consistent with Lionnet 2025's culminative-downstep/register reanalysis).

tone_statements.citation: Lionnet, Florian. 2025. Tonal languages without tone: downstep in Drubea and Numèè (Oceanic, New Caledonia). Phonology 42: e23. doi:10.1017/S0952675725100171
tone_statements.quote: The word-prosodic system of Drubea and Numèè is entirely built on one underlying binary contrast: registerless (i.e., prosodically unspecified) vs. downstepped elements. [...] Downstep is realised as a downward register contrast with what precedes. It is not realised utterance-initially [...] Finally, registerless elements are sensitive to utterance-final prosodic phenomena: final raising in Drubea, final lowering in Numèè. [...] One interesting property that emerges is CULMINATIVITY: a stem may include at most one downstep

sources.note: Kanak languages of the centre and far-south groups are tone languages with punctual (level) tones, unlike the contour tones of SE Asia; for nráa drùbea the tonal system is still hard to describe; two prosodic factors must be reckoned with, the isolated syllabic tone and a melody spanning several syllables; the language certainly has two level tones (high and low) but the syllabic tone is often modified by the intersyllabic melody; the system resembles the Japanese 'accentual' system. The talk itself focused on the Drubea tonal system.
